section.title: Jesus Greater Than Moses
section.sectionRationale: Moses was the towering figure of the old covenant, the servant faithful in all God's house. The writer honours him fully, then shows that Jesus is greater: Moses was a servant within the house, but Christ is the Son over the house, indeed its builder. This prepares the wilderness warning that follows.
section.thesis: Jesus and Moses were both faithful in God's house, but Jesus deserves greater glory, for Moses served as a faithful servant within the house while Christ rules as the faithful Son over it and, as builder, is greater than the house itself; and we are that house if we hold firmly to our hope.
section.frameNote: A tight comparison: the call to consider Jesus as apostle and high priest; the shared faithfulness of Jesus and Moses; the builder greater than the house; and the servant contrasted with the Son over the house, which is us if we hold fast.

units.label: Consider Jesus, apostle and high priest

verses.text: Therefore, holy brothers, who share in the heavenly calling, set your focus on Jesus, the {{apostolos|apostle}} and {{archiereus|high priest}} whom we confess.
He was faithful to the One who appointed Him, just as Moses was faithful in all God’s {{oikos|house}}.

units.label: The builder greater than the house
units.note: God is the builder of everything

verses.text: For Jesus has been counted worthy of greater glory than Moses, just as the builder of a house has greater honor than the house itself.
And every house is built by someone, but God is the builder of everything.

units.label: The servant and the Son over the house
units.note: we are His house, if we hold fast

verses.text: Now Moses was faithful as a servant in all God’s house, testifying to what would be spoken later.
But Christ is faithful as the Son over God’s house. And we are His house, if we hold firmly to our confidence and the hope of which we boast.

apostolos.gloss: One sent with authority as a representative, an envoy. Uniquely in the New Testament, Jesus is called the apostle, the one God sent to speak and act for Him, greater than Moses, whom God also sent to Pharaoh and to Israel.

archiereus.gloss: High priest, the chief mediator who represents the people before God. The letter's great theme: Jesus is the high priest we confess, combining in Himself the roles that were divided between Moses and Aaron under the old covenant.

oikos.gloss: A house or household, both the building and the family within it. God's house is His people; Moses served faithfully within it, but Christ, as builder and Son, rules over it, and believers are that house if they hold fast.

basic.context: Moses was the greatest figure of the Old Testament for Jewish readers, the one who led the exodus and received the law. The writer does not run Moses down; he calls him faithful in all God's house. But he shows Jesus is greater still. Moses was a servant in the house; Jesus is the Son over it and, as its builder, greater than the house itself.
basic.hermeneutics: The comparison draws on Numbers 12, where God calls Moses faithful in all His house. Read the argument through the images: servant versus Son, house versus builder. The conclusion is a call to hold fast, since we are that house.
basic.originalLanguages: Jesus is uniquely called the apostolos, the sent one, and the archiereus, high priest, of our confession. The recurring word is oikos, house or household: Moses served in the house, Christ is Son over the house, and we are that house.
basic.typology: Moses, the faithful servant and mediator, foreshadows Christ, the faithful Son and greater mediator. Moses' testimony pointed forward to what would be spoken later, fulfilled in the Son.
basic.christ: Christ is the apostle and high priest we confess, faithful like Moses but greater, for He is the Son over God's house and its very builder, sharing in the honour of God who builds all things.
basic.god: God appointed both Moses and the Son, and God is the builder of everything. He is faithful to His purpose, raising up servants and finally His Son to rule over His household.
basic.crossReferences: Numbers 12 calls Moses faithful in God's house. John 5 records Jesus saying Moses wrote of Him. 1 Peter 2 describes believers as a spiritual house.
basic.oneStory: God has always been building a house, a people for Himself. Moses served within it; the Son now rules over it as builder and heir, and all who hold fast belong to it.

context.literary:
The six verses are a single compact argument, and the word 'house' is the rope that ties it together, turning up in almost every verse. Verse 1 is the call, verses 2 to 6a are the proof, and verse 6b is the appeal. The call opens with 'Therefore', which links back to the end of chapter 2, where Jesus was called a merciful and faithful high priest. The writer picks up the second of those two words first. 'Faithful' is the pivot: it is said of Jesus in verse 2, of Moses in verses 2 and 5, and of Christ again in verse 6, so that the likeness is stated before the difference.

The form is the old rabbinic and Greek pattern of arguing from the lesser to the greater. Verse 2 states the likeness, verses 3 and 4 give a household principle that a builder outranks what he builds, and verses 5 and 6a apply the principle by pairing 'servant' against 'Son' and 'in' against 'over'. The little preposition matters: Moses served within the house, Christ rules over it. The key step is verse 4, a short aside that every house has a builder and that the builder of all things is God. The writer lets that line stand without comment, and the force of the argument rests on it.

The unit then turns suddenly in verse 6b with a condition, 'if we hold firmly'. That 'if' is the doorway into the long warning that follows, which runs from 3:7 to 4:13 and is built on Psalm 95. So this short paragraph does two jobs. It finishes the case for Christ's superiority, begun in chapter 1 with the prophets and the angels, and it opens the pastoral appeal that occupies the next chapter and a half. The BSB footnote at verse 6 notes that many manuscripts add 'firm to the end' after the boast of hope, a phrase that matches the wording of 3:14 and shows how scribes heard the two verses as partners.
context.historical:
For Jewish readers no figure stood above Moses. He had met God at the burning bush, brought the plagues on Egypt, led the people through the sea, mediated the covenant at Sinai, and received the pattern for the tabernacle, which Moses then set up, Exodus 40:33. The law was 'given through Moses', John 1:17, and the Old Testament closes its record of him by saying that no prophet since had known the LORD 'face to face', Deuteronomy 34:10. To lean back from Christ toward Moses would have felt, to threatened believers, like returning to something solid and honoured.

The writer therefore does not start with a criticism. He starts with the best thing God ever said about Moses, from Numbers 12:7: 'he is faithful in all My house'. That sentence was spoken in a crisis. Miriam and Aaron had challenged Moses' unique standing, and the LORD answered by naming him as a servant and then drawing a line between ordinary prophets, who received visions and dreams, and Moses, with whom He spoke 'face to face, clearly and not in riddles', Numbers 12:6-8. The first readers would have known that scene. The writer takes the highest compliment to Moses in the Torah and shows that it still leaves room for Someone greater.

'House' had several layers of meaning in Israel. It could be the sanctuary, as in the house of the LORD; the household of the people, as in the house of Israel; and the dynasty of a king, as in the promise that God would build David a house, 2 Samuel 7:11-13. All of these are in the background. Behind the first readers lay a long history in which a house for God had been built in stone, first as a tent and then as a temple, and in which the prophets had already warned that the Most High does not dwell in buildings made with hands, Isaiah 66:1-2. Stephen made the same point to hostile hearers, Acts 7:48-50.

Some in the early centuries read the word 'appointed' in verse 2 to mean that the Son was made like a creature. Athanasius and others answered that the verb, which in Greek can mean to make or to appoint, is used here of an office, as in 1 Samuel 12:6, where the LORD 'appointed Moses and Aaron'. The question is old, and the answer lies in the context, where the Son is called the builder of the house.
context.canonical:
The key text is Numbers 12:7, and Hebrews follows it closely. But the idea of a 'house of God' runs through the entire Bible, and the New Testament shows how the Son fulfils it. In the Old Testament, a house for God is first a tent in the wilderness, Exodus 40:34-35, then a temple built by Solomon, and then the people themselves, for the prophets speak of the 'house of Israel'. God's promise in 2 Samuel 7:13-14 to David that his son would build a house for His name, and that God would be his Father and he would be God's son, is quoted in Hebrews 1:5. Zechariah 6:12-13 speaks of a man called the Branch who 'will build the temple of the LORD', and who will be 'a priest on His throne', combining the builder, the king and the priest in one person.

The New Testament shows these promises fulfilled in Christ and then in His people. Jesus says, 'I will build My church', Matthew 16:18. Peter calls believers 'living stones' being built into a spiritual house with Christ as the living stone, 1 Peter 2:4-5. Paul says the church is 'God's household', built on the foundation of the apostles and prophets with Christ as the cornerstone, Ephesians 2:19-22, and tells Timothy that this household is 'the church of the living God', 1 Timothy 3:15. Hebrews 10:21 speaks of 'a great priest over the house of God'.

The Moses comparison is also developed elsewhere. John 1:17 sets the law given through Moses beside the grace and truth that came through Jesus Christ, and Jesus tells His critics that Moses wrote about Him, John 5:46. Moses had himself promised a prophet like him, Deuteronomy 18:15, a promise the New Testament applies to Jesus in Acts 3:22 and 7:37. Hebrews returns to the theme in 8:5 and 9:1 to show that the tabernacle Moses built was a copy and a shadow, and in 10:28-29 to argue that if rejecting Moses brought death, trampling on the Son brings far more.

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
The writer is not interested in a contest of rank for its own sake. He is answering a pastoral danger. The readers were Jewish Christians under pressure, tempted to feel that the Mosaic order was a surer thing than a Messiah they could not see, and he wants them to see that going back would mean turning from the very fulfilment that Moses served. Moses himself testified 'to what would be spoken later', so loyalty to Moses is best shown by listening to the Son.

He is careful with the praise. Nothing in these verses belittles Moses, and the comparison works only because Moses was truly faithful. That fits a writer who trusts the Old Testament as God's word and reads it as pointing beyond itself. What he wants the readers to carry away is a settled sense of where they live: not in the shadow of Moses but in the house the Son governs. The last clause is the aim of the whole piece. Being the house is a privilege and an identity, and the way it is lived out is by holding to confidence and hope. So the argument for the glory of Christ is meant to steady the nerves of tired believers.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription:
The first five verses are description. They say what Moses was and what Christ is, and they do not command anything except in verse 1, 'set your focus on Jesus'. Treat that as a real instruction: the verb asks for a careful, steady fixing of the mind, and the rest of the passage gives the reasons. The comparison of Moses to Christ is therefore not a recipe for how to rank leaders in the church, nor a licence to run down the Old Testament.

The last clause is the one prescriptive turn. It is not an instruction to earn a place in the house; it says that belonging shows itself in holding on. Care is needed in applying it. The condition describes how God's people are known and cautions those who drift, but the surrounding text is full of reassurance, since the same writer tells his readers that he is confident of better things in their case, Hebrews 6:9. Believers today are to hear both notes: confidence in what Christ has done, and the call to keep trusting Him rather than slide away.

debates.question: Does 'if we hold firmly' make our membership in God's house uncertain?

views.label: The 'if' marks the genuine believer
views.case: Those who truly belong to Christ do hold on, because God keeps them. Passages such as John 10:27-29 and Philippians 1:6 promise that no one can snatch the sheep from His hand and that He will finish what He began. On this reading the clause tells the readers how to recognize true faith, and the warnings are the means God uses to preserve His people.

views.label: A real warning to a real believer
views.case: Others hold that the warnings in Hebrews, including 6:4-6 and 10:26-31, are addressed to actual members of the community and describe a danger that is possible, so the 'if' marks a condition that the reader must meet. They read perseverance as something believers are called to and not merely evidence of a decision already made.

views.label: A corporate warning to a mixed community
views.case: A third view stresses that the letter addresses a congregation, and the wilderness generation that comes next included both the faithful and the faithless. The 'if' is then a call to every member to examine whether he shares in the house in reality and not only in name.

debates.bearing: All three views insist on the same response: hold fast. The passage gives no comfort to presumption and no reason for despair, and the persevering hope it asks for is what Paul calls being kept by God's power through faith, 1 Peter 1:5.

debates.question: Does verse 4, 'God is the builder of everything', say that Jesus is God?

views.label: Yes, the builder of verse 3 is the builder of verse 4
views.case: The argument runs from the builder of the house in verse 3, who is Jesus, to the builder of everything in verse 4, who is God. Chapter 1 has already called the Son the one through whom God made the universe, Hebrews 1:2 and 1:10, and John 1:3 and Colossians 1:16 say all things were made through Him. So the Son shares in the work and the honour of God the builder.

views.label: No, it is a general principle about God as source
views.case: Others read verse 4 as a plain aside that behind every house stands a maker, so that behind the house of God stands God the Father. On this view the verse protects the Father's place as the source of the whole building, and the Son's equality is taught elsewhere in the letter.

debates.bearing: The two views do not compete. The letter holds that the Father builds through the Son, so whoever reads verse 4 as an aside about the Father still finds the Son included in the building work by the rest of the letter.

debates.question: What does Moses' testimony 'to what would be spoken later' refer to?

views.label: The whole law as a shadow pointing ahead
views.case: Moses' work in tabernacle, sacrifice and priesthood was a pattern pointing to a reality still to come, as Hebrews 8:5 says. His faithful service gave testimony by building the shadow.

views.label: Moses' explicit promises
views.case: Others hear this as Moses' direct promise of a prophet like himself, Deuteronomy 18:15, and his writing about Christ, John 5:46.

debates.bearing: Both readings agree that Moses' faithfulness included a forward look. The older servant bore witness to the later Son, which is why the Son's greater glory fulfils Moses and does not displace him.

study.originalLanguages:
The command in verse 1 is katanoesate, 'consider', from a verb that means to fix the mind on something and take it in. Jesus uses it in Luke 12:24 and 12:27 when He tells His hearers to consider the ravens and the lilies. It does not mean a passing glance. The readers are asked to study Jesus as one studies something that will change how one lives.

The readers are called metochoi, 'sharers', of a heavenly calling. The same word is used in 3:14 of those who 'share in Christ', in 6:4 of those who have 'shared in the Holy Spirit', and in 12:8 of those who share in God's discipline. In Hebrews 1:9 the Son is anointed beyond His 'companions', and the word is the same. So believers are companions of the Son and not merely beneficiaries.

In verse 2 the phrase 'who appointed Him' is a participle of poieo, a verb that ordinarily means 'make' but can mean 'appoint' when an office is in view, as in 1 Samuel 12:6 where the LORD 'appointed Moses and Aaron'. The BSB renders the sense; the other possible English, 'made', stirred controversy in the early church. The tense matters as well. 'Faithful' is a present participle, so Jesus is described as faithful, not only as having been faithful.

The word for 'servant' in verse 5 is therapon, a different word from the common doulos for a slave. It is the word the Greek Old Testament uses in Numbers 12:7 and refers to a trusted attendant who serves in the household of someone important. The writer chooses it because it is the Old Testament's word for Moses, and it is a word of honour. 'Son' is huios, and the contrast between servant and Son, 'in' and 'over', is the hinge of the passage.

Verses 3 and 4 use kataskeuazo for building. It means to prepare, equip or construct, and Hebrews uses it for the setting up of the tabernacle in 9:2 and 9:6 and for Noah's building of the ark in 11:7. The perfect tense in 'has been counted worthy' in verse 3, exiotai, presents the worthiness as a settled fact. 'Glory' is doxa, the weight of honour, and the word 'honor' is time, the public value set on someone.

In verse 6 the closing words are parresia and kauchema. Parresia was once the citizen's freedom to speak openly in the assembly and in this letter it is the believer's open, unashamed access to God, as in 4:16 and 10:19, and Hebrews 10:35 warns against throwing it away. Kauchema is the ground of boasting. The word katecho, rendered 'hold firmly', means to hold down so that it cannot slip, and it returns in 10:23, 'let us hold resolutely to the hope we profess'. The mood is the subjunctive with 'if', which puts the clause in the realm of expectation and call, not of fact already settled.

typology.type: Moses, the faithful servant in God's house
typology.fulfillment: Numbers 12:7 records the highest praise the Torah gives Moses, 'he is faithful in all My house', and Moses was a mediator, a lawgiver and an intercessor who stood between God and the people. Hebrews does not abandon him; it says he was a witness to later words, verse 5. The escalation is from servant to Son and from a position inside the house to one over it. The type falls short in an obvious way: Moses was kept out of the land after he struck the rock, Numbers 20:12, while the Son brings His people in. Deuteronomy 34:10 also says no prophet has risen like him, and the New Testament says One has, Acts 3:22.

Moses finished the tabernacle, and the glory of the LORD filled it, Exodus 40:33-35. It was a house for God's presence, built according to a pattern shown on the mountain, Hebrews 8:5. In Christ the pattern gives way to what it represented: a household of people in whom God dwells. Peter calls believers living stones, 1 Peter 2:5, and Paul says they are being built together into a dwelling place for God in the Spirit, Ephesians 2:22. The type falls short because the tent held God's glory at a distance; Moses could not enter it when the cloud had settled, Exodus 40:35.

typology.type: The son who builds a house for God, 2 Samuel 7:13
typology.fulfillment: God promised David that a descendant would build a house for His name, and that God would be a Father to him and he a son. Solomon built the temple, but Hebrews 1:5 quotes the promise of Sonship and applies it to Jesus. In Zechariah 6:12-13 the Branch builds the temple and sits as priest on His throne. Jesus is the greater Son of David who builds a house of people, not stones, Matthew 16:18. The type falls short because Solomon's reign ended and his temple fell, while the Son's house is built to last forever.

Moses promised that the LORD would raise up a prophet like him from among his brothers, and told the people to listen to him. Acts 3:22 and 7:37 apply the promise to Jesus. The likeness is real: both mediate a covenant, both speak God's word, both lead a people. The escalation is that Moses spoke the word given to him, while Jesus is the Word through whom God has spoken in these last days, Hebrews 1:2. The type falls short because Moses could only point the people to the land, not take them into the rest, which is what the next chapters of Hebrews will say.

study.christ:
The passage leads to Christ by naming Him in a way that is almost a creed. 'Jesus, the apostle and high priest whom we confess' is a double title with a double direction. As apostle He is sent from God to us, the one who comes with God's own word and authority, as the Gospel of John says again and again. As high priest He goes from us to God, representing His people in the presence of the Father. These two movements are the whole of mediation, and Moses, who both brought God's word and interceded for the people, held something of both roles. In Jesus the two are held in one person.

The argument rests on a principle that is easy to miss. The builder of a house has more honour than the house, and so Jesus, who built the house, has more glory than Moses, who served in it. This claims much more than ordinary superiority. It says the Son is the builder of the very household in which Moses served. The earlier chapters have already said the Father made the universe through the Son, Hebrews 1:2, and that the Son is the radiance of God's glory and the exact representation of His nature, Hebrews 1:3. The writer is applying that to the household of God. When verse 4 says 'God is the builder of everything', the Son is not set outside that sentence. He is inside it as the One through whom the building is done.

The passage leads to Christ by contrast of position. Moses was faithful 'in' the house, as a servant who belonged to it. Christ is faithful 'over' it, as a Son who owns it. That is the difference between a trusted manager and an heir. It matches what Jesus said of Himself in the parable of the vineyard, where the owner at last sends his son. And it fits the promise to David that the Son would build the house, 2 Samuel 7:13.

It leads to Christ by fulfilment. Jesus said Moses wrote about Him, John 5:46, and that is what verse 5 means by Moses 'testifying to what would be spoken later'. So the Christian reads Moses not as a rival but as a witness. The more faithfully Moses did his work, the more clearly it points to the Son. To go back to Moses and away from Christ would be to ignore the testimony of Moses himself.

And it leads to Christ by what He makes of His people. 'We are His house.' The people of Christ are His dwelling, Ephesians 2:22, His building, Matthew 16:18, and His household. The reading must not be pressed into a code where every detail of the tabernacle becomes a hidden picture of Jesus. The writer's own interpretive moves are the limit: he reads Numbers 12:7 and shows the Son as the builder and the heir.
study.god:
Three things stand out about God in this short passage. First, He is the God who appoints. Both Moses and the Son were appointed, verse 2, and the God who builds also chooses the people who serve in His house. Nothing here is accident or self-promotion. The faithfulness of Moses and of Jesus is faithfulness to a commission given by God.

Second, He is the builder of everything. Verse 4 is a short sentence with a long reach, for it takes the claim of ownership beyond Israel and its sanctuary to the whole creation. Isaiah 66:1-2 asks what kind of house anyone could build for the One whose throne is heaven and whose footstool is earth, and Hebrews 11:10 calls God the architect and builder of the city for which Abraham looked. The God who is Himself the builder is not dependent on any house made by hands, and any house that is truly His is a house He makes. That is why the readers need not fear that leaving the old order leaves them without a home. They are in the house God builds.

Third, God is faithful and honours faithfulness. He praises Moses openly, 'he is faithful in all My house', and He does not let that praise go unrewarded. The attributes of God in this passage are consistent with His character in the Torah, where He speaks face to face with Moses and keeps His word. Yet God is also the God who places greater glory on the Son, so that His honouring of Moses does not exhaust His purpose. He is generous in His praise and unwavering in His plan.

There is also a trinitarian shape. The Father appoints, the Son is faithful over the house as its builder and heir, and the Spirit, who speaks in the next section through Psalm 95, Hebrews 3:7, will bring the word of warning. The passage does not explain the doctrine, but it takes it for granted in the way it speaks of the Father who appoints and the Son who builds.

For worship this means a deep security with an equally deep seriousness. God dwells with His people and calls them His house, so they are never homeless, and the house is built by One whose glory exceeds that of Moses and everything else. At the same time the house is the place of His holy presence, and its members are told to hold their confidence firmly. The proper posture is that of a household member who loves the Master's house and keeps the Master's word: glad, steady and watchful.

crossReferences.note: The text the writer is working from. Miriam and Aaron questioned Moses, and the LORD answered by calling him faithful in all His house and one with whom He speaks face to face. Reading the whole scene shows how high the praise is, and why Hebrews takes it seriously before pointing to One greater.

The final summary of Moses in the Torah says no prophet since has known the LORD face to face or done such signs. It explains why Moses held such honour, and why the claim that Jesus is greater would have been a bold one for first readers to hear.

Moses promised that God would raise up a prophet like him and told the people to listen. Acts 3:22 and 7:37 say Jesus is that prophet. The promise explains verse 5: Moses was a witness who pointed beyond himself to the one who would speak God's final word.

God promises David a descendant who will build a house for His name and be His son. The idea of a son who builds a house is the pattern behind verses 3 to 6, and Hebrews 1:5 quotes verse 14 of this passage in the first chapter.

A man called the Branch will build the temple of the LORD and will sit and rule on His throne as a priest. Here the builder of the house and the priest-king are the same person, which is just what Hebrews says of Jesus, both high priest in 3:1 and builder in 3:3.

Believers come to Christ the living stone and are themselves built into a spiritual house as a holy priesthood. It shows what 'we are His house' means in practice: a community of people, joined to Christ and offering worship, and not a structure of wood or stone.

Paul says Gentile believers are no longer strangers but members of God's household, built with Christ Jesus as the cornerstone into a dwelling place for God in the Spirit. It extends the house of Hebrews 3 to include people from every nation.

Jesus tells His critics that their accuser is Moses, in whom they hope, because Moses wrote about Him. It matches Hebrews 3:5 closely: a faithful Moses bears testimony to the later word, so refusing Christ means refusing Moses.

The opening of the letter prepares for the builder argument. God has spoken by His Son, through whom He made the universe, who is the radiance of God's glory and upholds all things by His word. The Son who builds the house is the one through whom everything was made.

The partner verse to 3:6. 'We have come to share in Christ if we hold firmly to the end the assurance we had at first.' Both verses use a condition in the same way, and read together they show that the writer sees holding on as the form real belonging takes.

The letter returns to the house and the confidence. 'We have a great priest over the house of God', and so believers may draw near, holding resolutely to the hope they profess. It shows that the call in 3:6 is a thread, not a single line, running to the end of the argument.

Moses finished the work of the tabernacle, and the glory of the LORD filled it so that he could not enter. It displays both his faithfulness and the limits of his position: he builds a house in which he cannot stand when the glory comes.

study.oneStory:
From the beginning God wanted a dwelling among His people. In Eden He walked in the garden with the man and the woman, and the sanctuary language of the Bible's first chapters shows that creation itself was meant to be His house. When sin drove humanity out, the story became the search for a way to bring God and people together again. The tabernacle was the first answer: a tent in the wilderness, built by Moses to a heavenly pattern, where the glory of the LORD came down, Exodus 40:34. Moses' faithfulness gave the people a place where God could live among them, and the Bible honours him for it.

But the tent was a copy and a shadow. The temple of Solomon followed, and the prophets said even that could not hold the God whose throne is heaven. The promise to David hinted at a better builder, a son who would build God a house and be loved as a son, 2 Samuel 7:13-14. When the temple fell and the people went into exile, the promise grew sharper, and Zechariah saw a Branch who would build a temple and rule as a priest on His throne.

Hebrews 3 says that the One has come. The Son is the builder of the house and its heir, so the house is no longer a structure of cedar and gold but a people. This is where the plot of the Bible turns. The glory that once filled a tent now fills a household of men and women, who are 'living stones' in a building whose cornerstone is Christ. The Old Testament is not set aside, for Moses' faithfulness set up the shadow, and the Son brings the substance.

The story also holds a caution that the Bible repeats. The wilderness generation, who had Moses as their leader, still failed through unbelief, and that is the subject of the very next verses. So the people of God are called to endure, to hold the confidence and the hope until the end.

The story ends with the house complete. John hears a loud voice from the throne saying that the dwelling place of God is with man and that He will dwell with them, Revelation 21:3. In that city there is no temple, because God and the Lamb are its temple, Revelation 21:22. The house the Son has been building throughout history is finished, and the household, gathered from every tribe and nation, lives in the presence of the God who built it.

quiz.q: How does the writer relate Jesus to Moses?

options.text: Both were faithful, but Jesus is greater, as the Son and builder over the house.
options.note: Verses 5 to 6 contrast the faithful servant with the faithful Son over the house.

options.text: Moses was a fraud and Jesus exposed him.
options.note: The writer honours Moses as truly faithful; the point is Jesus is greater still.

options.text: Jesus and Moses are exactly equal.
options.note: Jesus is counted worthy of greater glory than Moses.

options.text: Moses was greater because he came first.
options.note: Coming first does not make Moses greater; the Son surpasses the servant.

quiz.q: What is the difference between Moses' role and Christ's in God's house?

options.text: Moses was a servant in the house; Christ is the Son over the house.
options.note: Verses 5 to 6 draw exactly this distinction.

options.text: Both were merely guests in the house.
options.note: Moses served in it and Christ rules over it; neither is a mere guest.

options.text: Moses built the house and Christ only lived in it.
options.note: The reverse: Christ is the builder, greater than the house.

options.text: There is no difference in their roles.
options.note: The roles differ sharply: servant within versus Son over.

quiz.q: What are the two titles given to Jesus in verse 1?

options.note: He is the sent one and the mediating priest of our confession.
Those roles are true elsewhere, but verse 1 names apostle and high priest.
The titles are apostle and high priest, not servant and scribe.
He teaches and fulfils the law, but the verse names apostle and high priest.

quiz.q: What does verse 6 say marks those who are God's house?

options.text: Holding firmly to our confidence and the hope of which we boast.
options.note: Perseverance in hope marks genuine belonging.
It is holding to hope, not flawless performance, that is called for.
Belonging is by holding fast to Christ, not by ancestry.

options.text: A one-time decision with no continuing.
options.note: The emphasis falls on continuing to hold firmly.

questions: The writer urges us to fix our focus on Jesus. What competes for that focus in your daily attention?
Jesus is both the apostle sent from God and the high priest who represents us to God. How does holding both together enrich the way you relate to Him?
We are God's house if we hold firmly to our hope. What helps you keep holding on when your confidence feels thin?
Moses was faithful, yet only pointed forward to Christ. Are there good things or people you have let overshadow the greater Son?
Christ rules as Son over the household you belong to. How does living as part of His house shape your commitment to His people?

translationNotes.note: Jesus is called 'the apostle', the only place in the New Testament this title is given to Him; it names Him the authoritative one sent by God, paired with high priest.
The wording echoes Numbers 12:7, where God commends Moses as faithful in all His house; the writer takes up this praise to set the comparison.
Some manuscripts add 'to the end' to 'hold firmly', matching the similar phrase in verse 14 and underscoring perseverance.
